title.en: Hooke's law and the stress–strain curve

heading.en: Pull a spring, then pull harder

hook.en: Hang one coin on a spring and it stretches a little. Hang two and it stretches twice as much. But keep adding coins and one day the spring never comes back.
hook.kn: ಸ್ಪ್ರಿಂಗ್‌ಗೆ ಒಂದು ನಾಣ್ಯ ತೂಗಿಸಿದರೆ ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ ಹಿಗ್ಗುತ್ತದೆ, ಎರಡು ತೂಗಿಸಿದರೆ ಎರಡರಷ್ಟು. ಆದರೆ ನಾಣ್ಯ ಸೇರಿಸುತ್ತಲೇ ಹೋದರೆ ಒಂದು ದಿನ ಅದು ಮೊದಲಿನ ಸ್ಥಿತಿಗೆ ಮರಳುವುದೇ ಇಲ್ಲ.

objectives.en: Read the stress–strain curve of a metal
Tell ductile, brittle and elastomeric materials apart

narration.en: Hang one coin on a spring and it stretches a little. Hang two and it stretches twice as much. But keep adding coins and one day the spring never comes back.
narration.kn: ಸ್ಪ್ರಿಂಗ್‌ಗೆ ಒಂದು ನಾಣ್ಯ ತೂಗಿಸಿದರೆ ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ ಹಿಗ್ಗುತ್ತದೆ, ಎರಡು ತೂಗಿಸಿದರೆ ಎರಡರಷ್ಟು. ಆದರೆ ನಾಣ್ಯ ಸೇರಿಸುತ್ತಲೇ ಹೋದರೆ ಒಂದು ದಿನ ಅದು ಮೊದಲಿನ ಸ್ಥಿತಿಗೆ ಮರಳುವುದೇ ಇಲ್ಲ.

body.en: For small deformations, stress is proportional to strain: stress = k × strain. The constant k is the modulus of elasticity of the material. For a spring the same idea reads F = kx, where k is the spring constant.
body.kn: ಸಣ್ಣ ವಿರೂಪಗಳಿಗೆ ಪ್ರತಿಬಲವು ವಿಕೃತಿಗೆ ನೇರ ಅನುಪಾತದಲ್ಲಿರುತ್ತದೆ: ಪ್ರತಿಬಲ = k × ವಿಕೃತಿ. k ಎಂಬುದು ಸ್ಥಿತಿಸ್ಥಾಪಕ ಗುಣಾಂಕ. ಸ್ಪ್ರಿಂಗ್‌ಗೆ F = kx.

say.en: Load a metal wire slowly and plot stress against strain.
At first the graph is a straight line from O to A. Stress is proportional to strain: this is Hooke's law. A is the proportional limit.
Up to B, the yield point, the wire returns to its length when unloaded. B is the elastic limit.
Beyond B the deformation is plastic: a permanent set remains. D is the ultimate tensile strength, and the wire breaks at E.
If D and E are far apart the metal is ductile, like copper. If they are close it is brittle, like cast iron.
For a spring, Hooke's law reads F = kx. A spring with k = 200 newton per metre stretched by 5 centimetres pulls back with 10 newton.

narration.en: Load a metal wire slowly and plot stress against strain. At first the graph is a straight line from O to A. Stress is proportional to strain: this is Hooke's law. A is the proportional limit. Up to B, the yield point, the wire returns to its length when unloaded. B is the elastic limit. Beyond B the deformation is plastic: a permanent set remains. D is the ultimate tensile strength, and the wire breaks at E. If D and E are far apart the metal is ductile, like copper. If they are close it is brittle, like cast iron. For a spring, Hooke's law reads F = kx. A spring with k = 200 newton per metre stretched by 5 centimetres pulls back with 10 newton.

body.en: For a metal wire the graph is a straight line up to the proportional limit. Up to the yield point (elastic limit) the wire returns to its length when unloaded. Beyond it the deformation is plastic and a permanent set remains. The highest stress on the curve is the ultimate tensile strength, after which the wire necks and fractures. Ductile metals have a long plastic region; brittle ones break soon after the elastic limit. Elastomers such as rubber and the aorta stretch a lot but have no straight-line part.
body.kn: ಲೋಹದ ತಂತಿಯ ನಕ್ಷೆಯು ಅನುಪಾತ ಮಿತಿಯವರೆಗೆ ಸರಳರೇಖೆ. ಸ್ಥಿತಿಸ್ಥಾಪಕ ಮಿತಿಯ ನಂತರ ಶಾಶ್ವತ ವಿರೂಪ ಉಳಿಯುತ್ತದೆ. ಗರಿಷ್ಠ ಪ್ರತಿಬಲವೇ ಅಂತಿಮ ಕರ್ಷಕ ಸಾಮರ್ಥ್ಯ; ನಂತರ ತಂತಿ ತುಂಡಾಗುತ್ತದೆ. ತನ್ಯ ಲೋಹಗಳಿಗೆ ದೀರ್ಘ ಪ್ಲಾಸ್ಟಿಕ್ ಭಾಗವಿದೆ.

points.en: Proportional limit → yield point → ultimate strength → fracture
Ductile: long plastic region; brittle: very short
Elastomers: large strain, no linear region

heading.en: Read the curve left to right

body.en: The points on a stress–strain curve come in this order: Proportional limit, Elastic limit (yield point), Ultimate tensile strength, Fracture.
